{{Hatnote|1=Transcript of a [[Players Committee]] design question-and-answer stream.}}
'''Star Wars CCG Design Q&A''' (30 November 2015) is a 36-minute live question-and-answer session held by the [[Players Committee]] design team ahead of the release of [[Virtual Set 3]] on 4 December 2015. A design team member hosted, answering questions posted by players on the forum, and was joined by Tom Kelly of Design and Development (D&D). Participants: the host (Players Committee design team), Tom Kelly.

Source: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m-mTCWuHPqw Star Wars CCG Design Q&A], Star Wars CCG (Players Committee), YouTube (uploaded 30 November 2015).

''The text below is from the video's automatic captions, corrected for names and card titles; it has not yet been checked against the audio. Forum names of the players who asked questions are given as the captions render them. Words that could not be made out are marked [unclear].''

== Transcript ==
'''[00:05] Host:''' All right, I'm going to get started now. We don't have a lot of people watching on YouTube right now, but this will be saved and published to the SWCCG YouTube account to watch at a later date if you can't join us for the live discussion. I believe Tom Kelly is now on as well, to discuss some of the questions and the D&D happenings for this set. Tom, can you hear me? I can't hear Tom, so he's going to try to figure out his audio as we go. Let's just get started with the questions.

'''[00:50] Host:''' The first question comes from [unclear]: "What path of removal do you feel Light Side should take against [[Executor]] with [[Deflector Shield Generators (V)|Deflector Shield Generators]] and a pair of admirals, let's say Thrawn and Piett? Please consider in the answer how reasonably easy this is to set up." A lot of feedback from the playtesting team so far was that it helps against all paths of removal, and I think that's a valid concern. However, the device itself is not pullable right now, and it doesn't provide a whole lot of benefit against each of those different paths of removal. The power +2 is nice, and the immunity to attrition < 5 is good, but immunity < 5 doesn't help a card like the Executor. The weapon protection may be what you're concerned about: it protects from two of the biggest starship weapon interrupt helpers, Combined Attack and Power Pivot.

'''[01:55] Host:''' One comment we got from Development was that Dark Side could devote a lot of cards and a lot of Force in their setup to get the Executor in place at a system, usually with the steals getting worse all the time, and sometimes you just have to concede the system and try to beat them elsewhere. If you want to full-on attack an Executor that's fully loaded with this and with the admirals, it's going to be hard. You're going to have to out-power them some way. I think a lot of the Light Side capitals that we saw in this set could help to do that; we've seen some good stuff in playtesting from Admiral Ackbar and [unclear]. You can also add more to attrition if you get a second capital there as well, and you have to try to crack their immunity. Someone else suggested in the thread using Green Leader in Green Squadron 1, and that could be a good way of getting rid of one or two of the admirals. You could spin with Han, Chewie and the Falcon; that's a pretty good way to almost crack the immunity right there. So you have to be strategic with your play-making decisions as Light Side, and avoid them if you can. You may not be able to use Combined Attack anymore, but you might be able to go at them head-on if you want.

'''[03:05] Host:''' Thanks to everybody for posting the questions; there are a lot of good questions here, and I'll try to get to as many as I can. You're on about a one-minute delay, so if you post them, I'll try to get to them before the end. We should be live for another 25 minutes or so. We've got a lot of comments from Mike French; I don't really see a question, so I'm going to skip that. He makes some good points, good discussion points with the community, but I'm looking for specific questions right now.

'''[03:54] Host:''' More echoing concerns from a few others about Deflector Shield Generators. I trust Development, and there are going to be some options against it. As the Light Side player, I don't think it's as good as some people make it out to be, but it is supposed to be near the top of the power curve. One function that we actually took off, that it used to have in playtesting, was [unclear] to Used Pile for free, and we decided it was going to be useful in almost every game as it was anyway, so we took that off.

'''[04:30] Host:''' There's a question from Indiana Jones Jedi Knight. He talked a lot about this earlier in playtesting: [[The Force Is Strong With This One (V)|The Force Is Strong With This One]]. At first he was really excited to use it, and then he found in practice it was, in his words, kind of lackluster. "Can you explain how or why that text was settled on versus some of the other suggestions, and why it retained the I Have You Now cancel versus the [unclear] cancel?" We went back and forth on that a lot. There were two different targets we were looking at: which Light Side characters can we use this with, and which Dark Side cards can we use it against. Originally it said a Padawan or a Skywalker, I believe, and that was pretty broad: you could use it with any of the Lukes you had in your arsenal, and any of the Padawans, of which there are going to be more in the future. What concerned us there was using it with Luke Skywalker, Jedi Knight, who already has a lot of good synergy, especially with Like My Father Before Me.

'''[05:40] Host:''' The second part, using it against Dark Jedi: this works against any Dark Jedi, which would be Count Dooku, the Emperor, Vader, Maul. Whereas if you look at the Dark Side counterpart, I Have You Now, sure, it works with any Dark Jedi, but it only works against Rebels, so it's limited in that regard. One concern from Development was that this hits way too many Dark Side cards. We considered making it just the Episode I Dark Jedi, or possibly just the non-Episode I Dark Jedi, but we ended up going with non-Jedi Skywalkers and Padawans. This means you can do it with any Luke except Luke Skywalker, Jedi Knight, such as Luke Skywalker, Rebel Scout. Maybe this will encourage a little bit of the older Lukes as well, or a future Luke with ability less than six could work with it. And we wanted it to cancel I Have You Now, because we found I Have You Now was kind of a blowout card, and we didn't want this to be a blowout card where if you found it early and the opponent didn't have a [unclear], they lose. We tried to mitigate that blowout factor.

'''[06:50] Tom Kelly:''' Can you hear me now?

'''[06:52] Host:''' Yes, we can hear you now, Tom.

'''[06:54] Tom Kelly:''' Whoa, okay. I think it was the Windows 10 update or something.

'''[06:58] Host:''' I was just discussing The Force Is Strong With This One. Maybe you could give a little extra insight into why the text we have now was settled on, why it wasn't made a little more powerful, and why it kept the I Have You Now cancel.

'''[07:15] Tom Kelly:''' One of the things that we brought up was that there are two analogous Dark Side interrupts that we were looking at, obviously I Have You Now and Maul Strikes. I Have You Now is good against a certain subset of Light Side mains, and Maul Strikes is good against another subset, whereas we originally had The Force Is Strong With This One hitting every Dark Side main there was, and it was probably a little too strong. There are a lot of Dark Side decks that want to drop Vader at one site and the Emperor at another, and it was opening them up to overflow, so we reined it back to a more reasonable level. The other concern was that in the last couple of tournaments since Like My Father Before Me came out, we've seen that card in almost any platform you can think of, and we didn't really want to give Luke, Jedi Knight yet another tool when he seems like the defining ground character for Light Side right now. So that's why it's not quite as strong as we might have thought it would be originally, but I think it fits in a good place in the meta.

'''[08:35] Host:''' I agree. A second question from Indiana Jones Jedi Knight: "I understand the struggle, particularly with Imperial Entanglements, to balance the first-turn battle, but by making Light Side control a location at all times, any worry that games between Entanglements and this objective will take a bit longer, with the potential to flip each other back a lot? Do you think that line will still help keep [unclear] in the game against the objective?" Tom, do you want to start?

'''[08:58] Tom Kelly:''' Actually, this line of text was one that we debated literally until the last minute. It was the last change that we were going back and forth on in this set. You wouldn't think so at first, but the Light Side objective has actually been testing very well against Entanglements, even despite the fact that you expect to lose Tantive IV on turn one. So this control text is a way to balance the matchup a little more and give the Dark Side a chance going back and forth. Personally, I like games where each turn one player is flipping the other one back. That's good interaction: you're using all your sites, you're battling for resources. Sounds fun to me.

'''[09:40] Host:''' I agree, and I think we kept it on there because we wanted to encourage more interaction. We didn't want this to be a deck where you would turtle at one system or one site and never come back; you need to actually control some locations and spread out strategically. If Dark Side decides it's in their best interest to stop you controlling your location and flip you back for a turn, that means they're going to have to go to more locations, more battlegrounds. So I think all this is good, and as you mentioned, it has been testing very well against Entanglements so far. We want it to be an even matchup, and keeping this line there definitely makes it more even. I'm not too concerned about the time limits. If anything you're going to have more interaction and more cards on the table.

'''[10:50] Tom Kelly:''' It already starts a ship on the table, so the setup is already started, and that helps with that.

'''[10:58] Host:''' A third question from Indiana Jones Jedi Knight: "Setting aside Cad Bane, who is conditional, between Maul, Kanan and Padmé, why so much unconditional, splashable and blanket hate on immunity?" I'll start. First of all, I wouldn't call Maul, Kanan and Padmé unconditional, because they require you to be with one of your own characters or one of the opponent's characters, very specifically. Padmé can add a destiny to attrition with your other characters. Maul only works against a few of the opponent's characters, so if they're not playing those characters he doesn't do a whole lot. And Kanan was changed recently to work only with two other Rebels. So I don't think they're all unconditional. I do think they're splashable, and our focus for the Light Side cards here was to give Light Side some better support characters. We found that a lot of the time in building decks you have to choose: do I want Luke in space or Luke on the ground, Han in space or Han on the ground, Obi-Wan in space or on the ground. So many of those names are also the best starship pilots, so we wanted to give you more options to put other characters in, so you don't have to make a sacrifice in one of the theaters.

'''[12:10] Host:''' As far as blanket hate on immunity, I think "hate" is a strong word. Any time you can increase the chance of removing cards from the table, you're going to get more strategy involved. You're not going to see so much of just dropping a Dark Jedi alone and being okay for a while. We want some cards that will help you clear the opponent and move the game along a little bit, and that ties into the last point about time games. Adding more to attrition, which these cards and Ackbar do in some cases, is going to help the game move along a little quicker.

'''[12:58] Tom Kelly:''' And I'm not sure I would really call it an anti-immunity-to-attrition theme, because one of the big things that we're bringing back is the Home One package, and that's something that thrives on its high immunity. That's the reason people play it. Rebel Leadership as well. Limiting battle destiny, things like that: you're going to see some of those cards, but probably not all at the same time. I don't feel like immunity to attrition is going anywhere.

'''[13:25] Host:''' Let's make this one a quick one, Tom, because it has been around for a while: "Can you explain why no change to Dooku?"

'''[13:32] Tom Kelly:''' Well, I wanted there to be a change to Dooku. D&D was split on this. Some of us said let's just let him go, and some said it's probably not really good for the game. We were split, and I think that's probably the big reason we haven't seen anything yet. We don't have a mandate inside D&D to make this kind of change, and I don't think anyone thinks it's absolutely imperative. It would be nice if Dooku worked that way, but he's not breaking the game. The other thing is, let's see where everything falls. We've made a lot of changes; even the Decree being changed is pretty big for Dark Side mains decks, and maybe Dooku the way he is lets those decks be in the right place right now. We'll have to wait and see.

'''[14:20] Host:''' A question from [unclear]: "Why not reintroduce [unclear] that were able to deploy R3-T2 on Tantive IV on turn one? I never understood why [unclear] and their droids did not survive the Reset." Those cards were designed by the current Advocate. I loved the cards; I thought they were great, and they added different ways you could go when building decks starting with droids. I don't think this is the right time to reintroduce something like that. I can't speak to why it was not included in the Reset; I wasn't on the Reset strike team. But we don't want it to be extremely easy for Light Side to just move Tantive IV to Alderaan directly. This is always something we can add in the future.

'''[15:30] Tom Kelly:''' I just had to look up R3-T2 just now, and that seems like a pretty decent way. But probably the most common way we're going to see is starting a new Secret Base (V) to pull a system to move Tantive IV to before it gets to Alderaan, so there's going to be at least one stop in the meantime. Or we might see an Insurrection build using Docking and Repair Facilities [unclear] to get Tantive IV over. You might want to use the droid, but I'm not sure it's the most reliable option.

'''[16:05] Host:''' If there were a reliable way to get it, that could become another option. One other option we think is worth exploring is starting Squadron Assignments, getting out a ship with hyperspeed 5, and transferring R2 over there on the first turn. There are a lot of possibilities for how to build the deck, so I'm excited to see what players can do.

'''[16:30] Host:''' We've got a bunch of questions from [unclear]. These are good questions; I really like them. Tom, what cards had the most revisions or trouble within D&D?

'''[16:45] Tom Kelly:''' The objective, obviously. There's no doubt, and this has been true of pretty much every objective that I've worked on in my time in Development: it's the hardest to predict by looking at the text what it's going to do. I remember first seeing the Slavers objective; it was ridiculous, you had no idea. The same is true here. You just have to see how it works in playtesting and get a feel for the strengths of the deck, the weaknesses, where it's too good. I don't know how many versions this went through. Did you keep track?

'''[17:20] Host:''' Nope, I couldn't count. Double digits, I'm pretty sure. It was a lot. I think that's really the only card that stands out as something that gave us a lot of difficulty. A few went down to the wire, like we talked about already, Shield Generators and The Force Is Strong With This One, but I wouldn't say those gave us trouble like the objective did.

'''[17:45] Host:''' A second question: "How are foil AI [alternate image] cards chosen, and when will we know the others?" Honestly, they come along naturally. One thing we always look for is something that is affordable for players. We don't want to take something that's an expensive rare and put it on a common card. There was a lot of back and forth about the image for Darth Maul because of that. It came down to what was an appropriate image, what the rarity was, the ease of acquiring it, and something that would fit dramatically. It's mostly decided by the card designer, whether that's a player or a designer. Sometimes the Advocates will step in if they need to say we shouldn't do this one. Sometimes playtesters give a suggestion, and the graphics team has a big role.

'''[18:50] Tom Kelly:''' Just to illustrate, because the Maul story gets at what we're talking about: it was originally going to be on the Episode I [unclear], which is an uncommon from Coruscant, I think, and we thought that would be fine. Then somebody looked it up and found that there was only one in stock at Category One Games, so it wasn't as ubiquitous as we had thought, and we looked for other images. We had some cosplayer images, but it's not like a cosplayer as Grievous, where you don't see the face; the guy was recognizably not the same actor as Darth Maul. So we went back and forth on what image to use.

'''[19:40] Host:''' I haven't seen the PDF. The graphics team is working on it, and I don't want to look at it, because I want to be surprised myself. Being on D&D you miss out on the big surprise of a fully spoiled set, so I'm trying to enjoy the images. There might be an AI for Maul; I know the graphics team is doing some full-template cosplayer images, so there will definitely be some surprises. The whole graphics design team always does a good job.

'''[20:05] Host:''' The next question: "Has Drop! been an auto-include in playtesting?" I want to take this one, because this is technically my player card. This is a card that I really loved in Legacy; I played it in Bring Him Before Me. I was a huge fan of putting all your high destinies back. It was not an auto-include in playtesting; in fact it was far from it. A few people played it here and there, but everyone found it pretty underwhelming, and I can't wait to play it myself. We made a mirror for the Light Side as well; it looked like a pretty good mechanic for a mirror, and I like having an extra grabber in the game.

'''[20:55] Tom Kelly:''' That was a card that we briefly made better in the course of the design process, and we made it probably too good, to the point where it was an auto-include, and then we pared it back down to what it is now.

'''[21:08] Host:''' The next question: "If [Fives] is from one of the newer series, why not more fun information in the lore than just 'clone trooper'? More generally, when does D&D include other fun story text in keywords?" We actually can't do that. The only thing we're allowed to put into lore is card game mechanics. We can't put any extra storyline or fun flavor into it. We're limited to game terms: clone trooper and spy are two characteristics that have a gameplay meaning, so we can use those, but we can't add anything else. That's just a restriction on what we are allowed to do.

'''[21:45] Host:''' A rules question: "Can Diplomatic Mission deploy R2-D2 and C-3PO combos, including the new one in the set?" Yes. "Can it deploy R2-D2 in Red 5?" That is no. I had to ask this question myself earlier on, and I was told by Rules that anything that says to deploy a card aboard in this situation refers only to that character card and not to the other potential personas of it. I can't give you the full rules explanation, but the rules team has told me that you cannot deploy R2-D2 in Red 5 with the objective.

'''[22:30] Tom Kelly:''' I think it probably has to do with deployment restrictions. If it's an unpiloted starfighter, it has to deploy either to a docking bay or to capacity aboard a capital, and there are none of those on the table.

'''[22:45] Host:''' I'm going to defer to Rules on this one, but I know I was told that you cannot. Next: "What does the process look like for adding themes, the Black Sun material for example? Does D&D say something like we think the deck needs more characters or more locations and go from there, or did it start closer to 'we need more characters' and grow from that?"

'''[23:17] Host:''' From a design perspective, we look at things that we think could use some help, or that would be good for the meta. Black Sun is a fun, interactive deck that historically has been really [unclear], and we wanted to make a way to play it with more battlegrounds, so that's how we made these sites. One of its other weaknesses was space, and we thought this would be a cool way of giving Black Sun space a little bit of teeth. Some background on [[Falleen's Fist]]: it started out as a ship that was basically a person of force itself, so that you could deploy it to the Coruscant system and it would add the icons for you and it would become a battleground. Then it had a mechanic that whenever it died it was stacked under the system. That got kind of weird with Rules, and we decided we'd better just make a new Coruscant system that would start as a two but become a battleground when the Fist was there, or if the opponent took it over from you. We didn't want to leave Light Side stranded, where if they take out the Fist they're stuck at a two non-battleground.

'''[24:20] Host:''' As far as how we decide what to bring back, we're going to try to slowly bring some things back, but we're really going to try to focus on new material. If a deck in the future could really benefit from one or two helper cards, we might try to do that. Like this set: we decided to give Rebel Strike Team an extra scout and an effect that could get your sites out more easily. That's just two cards, and we'll see how Rebel Strike Team does. We don't expect it to be higher than tier two at the moment, but if someone finds something fun to do with it, in future we might add some more.

'''[24:55] Host:''' These are more questions for Development and Tom. "In testing, did Tantive IV live beyond turn two in most games?"

'''[25:00] Tom Kelly:''' We did a lot of testing for the Entanglements matchup, and in that build the answer is no. But against a lot of other things, yes, it's going to, because you've got the [unclear] R2 and 3PO, and that even covers a [unclear]. So most of the time, in matchups with other Dark Side decks that aren't Entanglements, we're going to see Tantive IV surviving. It's probably not even worth attacking Tantive IV a lot of the time, because all you're going to do is kill R2 and 3PO; they'll shuttle back up and move away. The best time to disrupt Tantive IV isn't during your turn one, but during turn two, when they move over to Coruscant, or wherever they choose to put their [unclear], a four or five system. That'll slow them down much more significantly.

'''[26:00] Host:''' We saw a lot of times that they would have a pit stop at some place like [unclear], and then if you attack and kill the droids, the plans go back to [unclear], which really sets them back. So attacking on turn one isn't really helping you a lot; turn two would be a lot more beneficial.

'''[26:20] Host:''' A question from [unclear]: "What's the intent of the new Maul's cancelling text? It seems like a [unclear] thing. Did you also find it to be helpful in other matchups?" Primarily it was helpful in [unclear], and the intent of the new Maul card in general was a more affordable Darth Maul, because Maul right now is one of the most expensive cards. We wanted something that would pack a little more punch, with a matching weapon. He may not be quite as good as [unclear] with a matching weapon, but I think he still stands up on his own. Hopefully we see him in some builds with some stolen lightsabers.

'''[27:15] Tom Kelly:''' One of the things that we saw even in Legacy was that when we had decks with [unclear] and Gift Of The Mentor that were playing Vader's Lightsaber and Dooku's Lightsaber, they were still playing [unclear] Maul because that's how efficient he is. This is just a way to try to make an alternative to that. It might be that people still just want to play that Maul, but this gives another option if you're worried about decks like that.

'''[27:55] Host:''' This Maul is really good against [unclear] as well. If that's something you expect to see, he might be a better choice. Question three: "Why did it feel necessary to create a Dark Side [unclear] and protect [unclear] instead?"

'''[28:31] Tom Kelly:''' Funny enough, we actually started it as a [Devastator] (V) and moved to the system. We felt it was a cleaner option, and we left some design space open in the future if the Devastator could be redone again. The primary reason was that we just wanted to fix one thing, which is Devastator against Throne Room with Squadron Assignments or something, where Throne Room goes, on their turn one activates five Force, plays something, kills Devastator, boom, the end. But we didn't want to let Entanglements start According To My Design, have the Emperor on the ground and Devastator in space, and be essentially immune in both theaters for their first turn. The way to do that was to put the text on the system. Now if Entanglements wants to run According To My Design, they're still going to worry about running up against Watch Your Step, which will convert their system, and Diplomatic Mission, which will convert their system, so they won't be able to rely on that game plan. That's why we switched from the ship to the system. It accomplishes the goals without making According To My Design stronger, at least we think.

'''[30:00] Host:''' Question four: "Why create a non-unique admiral?" Honestly, the primary reason is that there are virtually no other admirals that exist in the Star Wars universe for Light Side. I don't think making a non-unique one is a bad thing. It's interesting having it as two admirals so you can play a couple of them safely. It's a solid card by itself, it works with [[Rebel Leadership (V)|Rebel Leadership]], and that's enough to make it a pretty playable card. We didn't find any issues in testing with it being non-unique.

'''[30:45] Tom Kelly:''' One interesting thing is that there is now finally a Light Side card that cannot be deployed with [unclear], because it says ability less than three except for an admiral. I've always hated that text. I want to pull [unclear] on turn one.

'''[31:15] Host:''' A question: "How do we get the new Black Sun sites out? Are there going to be changes to the objective as well?" This was already answered: [Coruscant: Imperial City] (V) pulls the objective, which pulls another battleground site. Typically people have been playing Jabba's Palace to pull that, and now you can play Xizor's Palace sites. There will be no more changes to the objective itself. I think we have a pretty good chance in the future of adding more Xizor's Palace sites. That could be an interesting thing for a player-created card. We always like battlegrounds, so if you make it a battleground site, you've got a much better chance of it being included.

'''[32:00] Tom Kelly:''' Don't we need images for the Xizor's Palace sites?

'''[32:03] Host:''' That's in the works, but again, I'm trying to keep it from spoiling for myself. I do know we're going to have some custom images in this set, so never fear.

'''[32:15] Tom Kelly:''' Didn't we do this before, where we had a public call for some sites, and people went around and took pictures and submitted them?

'''[32:25] Host:''' I agree, I think that was a great thing. I always encourage that: if you ever want to submit an image for a card, contact anyone or post a message on the site. It's nice getting new, fresh energy in there, especially from players. I think that's all the questions we have. I was planning on being here until around five, so that's pretty good timing. Tom, do you have anything else you want to add?

'''[33:00] Tom Kelly:''' No, I think the set looks good. It's been great working with all the design team, and I'm ready for the next one.

'''[33:08] Host:''' What's your favorite card in the set?

'''[33:10] Tom Kelly:''' Honestly, I think it's [[Wild Karrde]]. I really think that's a cool ship, and I'm hoping that it might open up a non-Squadron Assignments-based Watch Your Step, between that and [unclear] and maybe other things: an alternative that's more ground-focused, with random ships with smugglers on them. Nobody's really gone over the moon about it yet, but I think it's a really cool card.

'''[33:45] Host:''' I agree. I was thinking the same thing when I first saw it: maybe we can get away from Squadron Assignments in Watch Your Step a little bit. The obvious answer for my favorite card would be my Drop! card, but I'm not going to take the easy way out. I think my favorite card in the set is probably [[Cad Bane]]. I really like how Cad Bane tested and how he's helped out Black Sun a lot. He's a pretty powerful bounty hunter. I always like playing Black Sun myself, and then not being able to clear Luke, Jedi Knight, you just think as a Black Sun player, what do I do now? It's pretty cool to me that you have a nice Cad Bane coming out who can get more characters off the table.

'''[34:45] Tom Kelly:''' He fits in with the whole Black Sun theme of alternate ways of getting people off the table. They're not going to overpower you; they're going to get you with tricks. He's not my design, but he's a very good card. I like him.

'''[35:01] Host:''' All right, thanks, Tom. I appreciate you helping out, so I didn't have to talk for half an hour straight, and thanks for the questions you sent in. This will be published on the Star Wars CCG YouTube page, so you can watch it again any time. Thanks to the players; I hope you really enjoy the set.
